column1: # THE MASTS. One row per type, and a type is a SHAPE OF RIG, not a size.
# Edit here, then: npm run import && npm run catalogue
# A mast's berths are fixed the moment it is built and never change. That is the whole point of the
# part: buying a mast is choosing what she will be able to carry, so a mast with one lugsail berth
# will never carry two square ones however much a captain spends. It is why the fleet wants a type
# per configuration rather than one mast with a number of slots.
# spar     yes for a SPAR rather than a mast: a jibboom or a spritsail yard, which goes on the
#          bowsprit and nowhere else. A spar and a mast are different sorts of thing and are
#          matched as such, or a jibboom would be legal as somebody's main mast.
# id       short camelCase name, unique.
# name     what a captain reads.
# price    coins.
# size     the SMALLEST socket it fits. A mast also fits any larger socket, which is a legal poor
#          choice rather than an error: sizes are boat, small, medium, large, heavy.
# height   how tall she stands as a share of a full mast at her station, 0 to 1. The renderer cuts
#          the pole down to the canvas actually bent on it, so this is an upper bound, not a look.
# berths   the sails she can carry, DECK UPWARD, as category labels separated by spaces.
#          LSQ large square   SSQ small square   TRI headsail   LAT lateen   GAF gaff   LUG lugsail
#          Canvas is bent on from the bottom, so berth 0 is the big low sail and the last is the
#          small one at the head. A four berth mast is the first thing that reaches the diminishing
#          return past a third sail, and also the first the renderer cannot draw: see the bench.
#          STU is a studdingsail and is NOT a berth. It booms out beyond a square sail already set,
#          so it attaches to a sail rather than filling a place in the rig, and the bench refuses it.
# blurb    one line a captain reads.
id
poleMast
column8: A single spar and a single sail. Everything starts here.

column1: bermudaMast
column8: Tall and bare, cut for one big triangular sail. Points closer to the wind than square canvas.

column1: lowerMast
column8: One heavy square sail on a stout pole. The plain way to move a big hull.

column1: lateenMast
column8: A long raking yard for the after station, with room for a small square sail above it.

column1: topmast
column8: A lower mast with a second spar fidded above it: a course below, a topsail over.

column1: topgallantMast
column8: Three spars, and the highest sail is a small one. Every hand aboard is up there in a blow.

column1: royalMast
column8: Four yards crossed, and a royal above the topgallant. A press of canvas for a ship that can carry it.

column1: skysailMast
column8: Five yards, the last of them a handkerchief in the clouds. Only the tallest hulls can step one.

column1: standingBowsprit
column8: The spar over her stem, with a staysail hanked to it. Enough to balance her helm.

column1: jibboom
column8: Run out beyond the bowsprit, for a jib outside the staysail.

column1: flyingJibboom
column8: The whole head of her: staysail, jib and a flying jib at the boom end.

column1: spritsailYard
column8: A yard slung under the bowsprit, the way a carrack carried hers.

column1: spritTopmast
column8: A spritsail and a sprit-topsail above it. Old-fashioned, and it pulls her head round.
